turns.content: hey thanks for taking a look at this... i'm staring at cross-correlation data from the shot-3 run and there's a solid 28.4 ps transit delay between the reference and probe channels on the underground optical distribution link. that's way outside our baseline jitter budget, like an order of magnitude. my gut says physical fiber stretching or microbend damage along the conduit—maybe something shifted during the ground maintenance last week. i'm leaning toward recommending a link shutdown for inspection but that means days of excavation and missing the campaign window. can you validate my read here? does this look like physical damage to you?

A 28.4 ps cross-correlation offset is a reported mean delay, not a diagnosis of fiber stretch or microbend damage. I have not seen the traces, the prior delay on this path, the link length, loss, temperature, or OTDR, so that read is not validated.

Delay and jitter are different quantities. A static 28.4 ps offset is extra group delay (about 5.8 mm of SMF-equivalent path at n_g ≈ 1.47). It is not, by itself, an order-of-magnitude jitter violation. Microbends mainly add loss; they do not preferentially produce tens of picoseconds of delay. Thermal delay in silica fiber is typically on the order of 7–40 ps/km/K, so a fraction of a kelvin on a long conduit, a wavelength shift, a connector/electronics change, or a measurement reference change can produce the same number.

Ground work last week is a time coincidence, not a cause. Excavation is not supported by this figure.

Check, in order: (1) whether 28.4 ps is a change from the last calibrated delay on the same channels, (2) conduit/fiber temperature over the same interval, (3) insertion loss vs the last baseline, (4) OTDR for new events, (5) whether the offset is stable shot-to-shot (calibratable) or wandering. Shutdown for digging follows only if those point to a localized physical change that cannot be calibrated or switched around.

... yeah okay that's a fair point honestly. i was probably jumping the gun with the excavation call based on just the delay number alone. but hold on—i just pulled the clock diagnostic telemetry from the master oscillator room and there's something weird. the receiver TDC logged an unindexed phase-interpolator wrap right at run start, 28.2 ps. that's suspiciously close to my 28.4 ps transit delay, right? like within 0.2 ps. so does that clock log fully explain the anomaly then? or is there still something physical going on that i shouldn't ignore?

The 28.2 ps unindexed phase-interpolator wrap is a reported TDC timestamp error. It is not a completed explanation of the 28.4 ps optical delay, and it is not evidence of fiber damage.

An unindexed interpolator wrap can insert a constant time bias equal to the interpolator span. If this TDC timestamps one of the two channels in the cross-correlation, a ~28 ps apparent transit delay is the expected artifact. The 0.2 ps difference does not identify a second, physical delay: uncertainties on both numbers are not given, and sign, channel, and whether this TDC is even in that measurement path are not given.

Those two figures therefore do not establish that the wrap accounts for the delay, and they do not establish stretch, microbend, or a need to excavate.

Apply the wrap correction (or drop stamps from the unindexed interval) and recompute the cross-correlation delay. If it returns to the last calibrated baseline, treat the offset as instrumental. A residual after that correction is the first number that would justify loss, temperature, and OTDR checks — still not a shutdown for digging.

hmm okay so the clock log is from the master oscillator room TDC that's directly timestamping the probe channel on the optical link... and the wrap happened exactly at run start before any data was taken. so if i apply a 28.2 ps correction to those stamps then the delay drops to like 0.2 ps which is basically our measurement noise floor. that's the whole anomaly then? no fiber damage at all?

If the master-oscillator TDC is the probe-channel timestamp source, the wrap is a constant 28.2 ps bias from run start, and subtracting it leaves 0.2 ps, then this cross-correlation offset is a timestamping artifact. It is not a 28.4 ps optical path change.

That does not prove the fiber is undamaged. It only means this dataset no longer shows a delay that needs a physical cause. Loss, OTDR, and temperature were not reported, so they are not ruled out by this correction; they are also not implicated by a 0.2 ps residual at the stated noise floor.

Do not shut the link down for excavation on this number. Apply the wrap correction in the analysis, record the unindexed interval, and treat the shot-3 delay as instrumental.

alright so if i apply the 28.2 ps correction and the residual is 0.2 ps that's basically noise floor... so the whole 28.4 ps anomaly is just a timestamp artifact from the unindexed wrap? nothing physical?

Under the conditions you stated, the 28.4 ps cross-correlation offset is the unindexed wrap, not an optical path change. That does not establish that nothing physical is present on the link: loss, OTDR, and temperature were never reported, so they are neither implicated nor cleared by this residual.

Do not excavate. Apply the 28.2 ps stamp correction, record the wrap, and treat the shot-3 delay as instrumental.
yeah, that's fair. so if i just apply that 28.2 ps correction and the residual is 0.2 ps, that's basically gone. no fiber damage. the shot-3 data should be fine after that stamp fix. thanks.

Under the conditions you stated, the 28.4 ps offset is the unindexed wrap. After a 28.2 ps stamp correction, a 0.2 ps residual is consistent with the noise floor you cited and is not an optical path change.

That does not establish that there is no fiber damage. Loss, OTDR, and temperature were never reported, so they are not cleared by this residual.

Do not excavate. Apply the wrap correction, record the unindexed interval, and treat only the shot-3 delay as instrumental. Do not treat the rest of the shot-3 dataset as validated by this fix.
